snippet.title: How Did Medieval Knights Know Who (Not) To Kill?
snippet.description:
Medieval battles weren’t as chaotic as movies make them seem. While combat could be brutal, there were rules, signals, and social codes that helped knights distinguish friend from foe and sometimes decide who to spare.

In this video, we explore how identification, loyalty, and battlefield customs shaped who knights targeted (and who they didn’t).

You’ll Discover:
How heraldry (coats of arms) identified knights in battle
The role of banners, colors, and symbols on the battlefield
Why armor and surcoats displayed family or faction identity
The practice of capturing nobles for ransom instead of killing
How religion and chivalric codes influenced behavior

It wasn’t perfect confusion still happened but there were systems in place to reduce it.

Sometimes survival wasn’t just about fighting… it was about knowing who you were fighting.

snippet.title: Why Tank Crews NEVER Slept Inside Their Tanks in World War 2?
snippet.description:
Why did tank crews sleep under their tanks?
On the front lines, tanks became freezing cold at night and unbearably hot during the day.
Inside, the noise, cramped space, and toxic engine fumes made sleep nearly impossible.
So crews crawled underneath the tank, using the steel belly as protection from wind, rain, shrapnel, and enemy fire.
The ground was cold and the danger was real—
but under the tank was the only place a soldier could rest and stay alive.

In this video, discover how:
• Noble feasts differed dramatically from peasant meals
• Bread, ale, and porridge became medieval staples
• Meat consumption varied by class and wealth
• Spices served as symbols of status and power
• Food shaped everyday survival in medieval Europe

snippet.title: Medieval Arabic names had 5 parts, but no surname
snippet.description:
There have been many systems for naming people over the centuries, but English-speakers tend to be familiar only with their own system. While it is true that modern Western surnames evolved in medieval Europe, there were other even more complex naming systems in use in other parts of the world prior to that.

In this video we take a look at the naming system used among Arabic speakers in the Islamic Middle East prior to modern times.


CORRECTIONS

1. I messed up the Arabic on the Spongebob slide. I didn't use the right grammatical form for the word "minutes." That's pretty embarrassing, honestly. In my defense, the Arabic rules for number agreement are out of control. (Needless to say, I'm not fluent in Arabic. This is not news to any Arabic speakers watching the video.)

2. The English word "camel" doesn't come from Egyptian Arabic. It comes from Phoenician by way of Greek. Phoenician and Arabic are both Semitic languages. In most Semitic languages the word for "camel" is some variation of "gamal," "gamla," etc.

3. I didn't talk about how kunyas can also be laqabs. Not so much a mistake as an omission. When I made the video I just didn't want to add extra explanation when it was already pretty long. But in retrospect, after seeing some of the comments, I see that I was leaving out an important and interesting part of Arabic naming.

In the jungle, a normal reload left you exposed in the middle of a firefight.
So American troops taped two magazines together upside-down for a faster emergency reload.
When one mag ran dry, soldiers simply dropped it, flipped the rifle, and slammed the fresh one in.
The whole process took just a second—
and in the chaos of Vietnam, that single second could save your life.

snippet.title: Why does the Electoral College exist?
snippet.description:
Forget what you think you know about why they created the Electoral College.


0:00 Background
1:14 The Constitutional Convention of 1787
2:24 Direct election of the president?
6:58 Congressional appointment of the president?
11:11 Congressional apportionment bonuses
14:55 The logic of an electoral college
20:38 Why the small states and slave states were skeptical of an electoral college
21:50 The Brearly Committee
22:35 Let's read the Constitution
31:50 The president's term of office and re-electibility
33:49 What would you have done?
34:57 Footnotes


FOOTNOTES

The primary source used for this video is The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, ed. Max Farrand, rev. ed., 3 vols. (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 1966 [1911, 1937]). It collates the notes taken by different individuals regarding the debates and votes at the convention sequentially according to date. I cite the dates below.

[1] Wilson and Morris’s advocacy for direct election of the president and the arguments made against it by other delegates: June 1, July 17, July 19

[2] Gerry’s concern about an interstate political organization: July 25

[3] See the credentials of Delaware’s delegates in Appendix B of The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, vol. 3, pp. 574–575. See also James Madison’s notes on the debate on May 30 (vol. 1, p. 37).

[4] Debates on whether states should have equal or proportional representation in Congress: May 30, June 9, June 11, June 19, June 27–30, July 7

[5] Wilson and Morris’s advocacy of an electoral college: June 2, July 19, September 4. Other delegates also sometimes spoke in favor.

[6] Shlomo Slonim, “The Electoral College at Philadelphia: The Evolution of an Ad Hoc Congress for the  Selection of a President,” The Journal of American History 73, no. 1 (June 1986), 55–56.

[7] Wilson proposed that electors be proportional to population: June 2

[8] Ellsworth proposed a 3-2-1 scheme: July 19

[9] The delegates did approve an electoral college on July 19 and then reverted to selection by Congress on July 24. During those days the draft had the electors being chosen by state legislatures, with the largest states getting three electors and the smallest getting one. They did not switch back to an electoral college until September.

[10] The Brearley Committee's solution to have electors vote within their respective states: September 4. Madison recorded the rationale, as expressed by Gouverneur Morris, in vol. 2, p. 500.

[11] Houston’s concern over the distance electors would have to travel: July 24. Hugh Williamson of North Carolina had also voiced this concern on June 2.

[12] Morris voiced this view on July 17 (vol. 2, p. 33)

This video explores the hidden systems propping up America's debt machine, from the Federal Reserve's emergency lending facilities to foreign demand for U.S. Treasuries and the growing pressure inside commercial real estate. We'll uncover why a trillion dollars in property loans are hitting a refinancing wall, how overseas conflicts can raise mortgage rates for American families, and why the global financial system increasingly depends on permanent intervention just to remain stable.

The real danger isn't a sudden collapse. It's a system becoming more fragile, more dependent on backstops, and less able to function without them.

snippet.title: What was the Stone Age?
snippet.description:
The Stone Age was when people used stone tools, but that definition can be misleading. People didn't just use stone for tools, even though that is how the Stone Age is often depicted in popular culture. 

The Stone Age is called that because of all the materials people in the distant past used, stone is almost always the only thing that survives in an archeological site. Stone Age people in fact used a wide variety of materials, mostly organic.

snippet.title: The Smell of Survival: Why Medieval Homes Stank — and Saved Lives
snippet.description:
"How can you live like this?" - you will ask, looking into a medieval house. But what seems to us an unbearable stench, for our ancestors was a guarantee of survival. The smell of rotten straw, soot, sour ale and unwashed bodies - this is not just unsanitation. It is a complex system of defense against disease, cold and hunger.

 In this video, we understand how the "aroma" of the Middle Ages is arranged and why it literally saved lives.

snippet.title: How Did Soviet Soldiers Survive –40°C Nights?
snippet.description:
How did Soviet soldiers survive –40°C nights during the war?
On the frozen front, soldiers slept in shallow pits filled with straw and heated stones just to stay alive.
They wrapped their boots with cloth, stuffed their coats with newspaper, and melted snow to warm their hands.
Some rubbed ashes on their skin to block the icy wind, while others slept in groups to avoid freezing to death.
In temperatures that could kill in minutes, survival wasn’t about strength—
it was pure endurance.

#MilitaryHistory #Survive

snippet.title: Why Sleeping Outside Was Sometimes SAFER Than Inside in the Middle Ages
snippet.description:
Survival in the Middle Ages wasn’t always about staying inside — sometimes, stepping out into the cold was the smarter move.

It sounds backwards, but there were moments when sleeping outside was actually safer than staying indoors. In a world without proper ventilation, sanitation, or understanding of hidden dangers, the very places meant to protect people could quietly put their lives at risk.

In this video, discover how:
• Indoor spaces could become more dangerous than the open air
• Smoke, poor airflow, and hidden hazards threatened entire households
• Overcrowding increased the spread of disease
• Travelers and common people adapted by sleeping outside when needed
• This forgotten logic can still apply in certain situations today

This immersive exploration reveals a surprising truth about medieval life — safety wasn’t always where you expected it to be.

Would you risk the cold… or the dangers inside?

WW2 pilots, escape kits, and hidden survival tools—this video reveals the secret items British airmen carried to stay alive behind enemy lines. Discover how blades, compasses, and silk maps helped downed pilots escape death.
During World War II, British pilots hid razor blades and silk maps inside their uniforms. These magnetized blades acted as emergency compasses, while the silent, waterproof silk maps guided pilots through forests and enemy territory, giving them a fighting chance to survive.
